gaps.description: The suite tests conversions in assignments, calls, returns, literals, statements, and many explicit forms, but never the source-level &*p form. Go gives &*p the unnamed type *T even when p has a named pointer type P; nilness and identity must also be preserved.
gaps.evidence: The combined mutant removed the dedicated compiler conversion for ast.StarExpr. It passed every original new-mode test and the full base mode. On the probe it reported `reflect.TypeOf(&*p) = ptrconv_658733.ptcIntPtr, want *int`, lost identity, and produced the named type for the nil form. The reference implementation passed the same probe.
gaps.probeDescription: Create p of named type ptcIntPtr, evaluate q := &*p, and assert reflect.TypeOf(q) is *int, q aliases &n, conversion back equals p, and the nil form is a nil *int.
gaps.title: No coverage for &*p when p has a named pointer type
gaps.wrongImplDescription: Translate &*p by returning p unchanged, an attractive simplification based on the usual &*p identity rule, without noticing that the result's required pointer type differs for a named p.

gaps.description: Existing unsafe tests verify target-typed reads and scalar writes, and aggregate tests cover scalar aggregate members. They do not write a non-nil named pointer through a reinterpreted **T. Thus they miss an implementation that converts getters but stores setter values unchanged, leaving an original *int variable holding the wrong pointer representation.
gaps.evidence: The combined mutant replaced the generic converted-pointer setter with a direct store. It passed the complete original new and base suites. The reference passed the probe; the mutant failed with `write through **ptcInt did not leave an *int pointing at m`. Aggregate pointer-field/element probes also established that this gap is specifically the untested direct nested-pointer setter path.
gaps.probeDescription: Convert &p, where p is *int, through unsafe.Pointer to **ptcInt; assign (*ptcInt)(&m) through it; then require p == &m, *p == 2, and equal unsafe addresses.
gaps.title: Unsafe nested-pointer writes are not checked for conversion back to the original variable type
gaps.wrongImplDescription: Build the target-typed proxy getter correctly but implement its setter as `ptr.$set(v)` rather than reinterpreting v to the source pointee type. This is a natural one-way-conversion shortcut and still passes scalar tests where JavaScript representations coincide.

gaps.description: The suite checks reflection addresses of struct fields, array elements, and slice elements, but not Elem().Addr() starting from a named pointer. The reflected address must be the unnamed *T and canonicalize to the same variable/address.
gaps.evidence: After removing the reflect Elem pointer canonicalization, while retaining the rest of the reference reflection machinery, the original new suite passed; the combined mutant also passed the full base suite. The oracle path passed the probe, while the mutant failed `reflect Elem().Addr() did not return *int at p's address`.
gaps.probeDescription: For p of type ptcIntPtr, evaluate reflect.ValueOf(p).Elem().Addr(); assert its type is *int, its interface is an *int equal to &n, and its unsafe address equals p's address.
gaps.title: No coverage for reflection's Elem().Addr() on a named pointer
gaps.wrongImplDescription: Implement compiled &*p conversion and general reflected addresses, but omit the special conversion in reflect.Value.Elem for named pointer values, reusing the named pointer representation as the address of the element.

output.taskSummary: The task asks GopherJS to make pointer conversions behave as they do in Go: explicit and implicit conversions should preserve the identity of the pointed-to variable and produce the destination pointer type; nil must stay nil; conversions through unsafe.Pointer and reflect must work for named and structurally corresponding types; and reads through an unsafe-converted view use the view's type while writes still affect the original variable. The new-mode harness runs the added Go tests under GopherJS in two packages. The tests cover direct conversions, implicit conversion contexts, pointer equality and nil, unsafe.Pointer, arrays and structs, and the reflect APIs named by the prompt.

tests.verifies: A reflect.MakeFunc function declared to return ptcIntPtr accepts a returned reflect.Value of *int and, when called, produces ptcIntPtr equal to &n; a returned nil *int produces nil ptcIntPtr.

tests.evidence: The prompt names NewAt and explicitly covers arrays made from types differing only by name, target-typed reads, writes retaining the original variable type, and exact identity.
tests.name: TestPtrConvReflectNewAtArray
tests.qualityCheck: Fair but one array length/type representative; other tests add differing shapes and lengths.
tests.verifies: reflect.NewAt([2]ptcInt64, &a) returns *[2]ptcInt64 whose second element and reflected Elem().Index(1).Interface() have the named ptcInt64 type and value 2; writing q[0] updates the original int64 array while its element remains type int64; and both unsafe conversion directions preserve the array address.

tests.evidence: The prompt expressly includes addresses returned by reflect in the same-variable equality requirement and requires the converted pointer to refer to the exact variable.
tests.name: TestPtrConvReflectAddresses
tests.qualityCheck: Fair; covers reflect-address sources for fields and indexed elements. The struct field is exported where Interface is used, avoiding a hidden visibility condition.
tests.verifies: For a reflect field, UnsafeAddr converted to unsafe.Pointer equals &s.n and Addr().Pointer equals UnsafeAddr; converting the reflect field address and direct field address to *ptcInt64 yields equal pointers; reflect addresses for an exported struct field, array element, and slice element equal the corresponding Go addresses and named-pointer conversions compare equal.

tests.evidence: The prompt includes arrays and types differing only by name, requires target-typed reads and original-typed writes, and requires exact identity for the pointed-to variable.
tests.name: TestPtrConvUnsafeSliceElements
tests.qualityCheck: Fair but focused on one element type and slice length; array and struct view tests provide additional coverage.
tests.verifies: unsafe.Slice built from *ptcInt64 over an int64 array reads element 3 as ptcInt64, writing element 1 changes the original int64 value while its type remains int64, and &sl[1] equals the converted address of &a[1].

tests.evidence: The prompt names reflect Set and requires destination type, exact identity, and nil preservation for pointer conversions.
tests.name: TestPtrConvReflectSetArrayPointer
tests.qualityCheck: Fair but limited to one non-nil array pointer and two nil cases.
tests.verifies: reflect.Set from *[3]int to ptcArrPtr produces the named pointer type and same array address; Set from nil *[3]int stores nil; and Set from nil *ptcArr to ptcNamedArr stores nil.

tests.evidence: The prompt covers structs and nested values whose types differ only by name, requires target-typed reads and writes retaining the original variable type, and invites similar reflect operations beyond the listed examples.
tests.name: TestPtrConvReflectSwapper
tests.qualityCheck: Fair; this is a useful integration test of a standard reflect operation on the converted view.
tests.verifies: reflect.Swapper applied to the slice of ptcInner2 values viewed over ptcInner values swaps the original two structs; the original field remains type int64, while the viewed first field has type ptcInt64 and value 2.

tests.evidence: The prompt explicitly says zero unsafe.Pointer counts as nil and that the converted pointer is nil iff its source is nil, including named struct pointer types.
tests.name: TestPtrConvUnsafePointerNilStruct
tests.qualityCheck: Fair, though redundant with the earlier nil/unsafe-pointer coverage. Keeping this test last is a harness safety precaution and does not make its assertion depend on earlier tests.
tests.verifies: A zero unsafe.Pointer converts to nil *ptcStruct, and a nil *ptcStruct round-tripped through unsafe.Pointer converts to nil *ptcStruct2.

tests.evidence: The prompt covers conversions via unsafe.Pointer, including element types differing only in name and arrays/structs composed of such types, and requires target-typed reads, original-variable writes, exact identity, and zero-unsafe-pointer nil behavior. `upUnsafe` is defined from unsafe.Pointer, so it exercises that named form.
tests.name: TestPtrConvNamedUnsafePointer
tests.qualityCheck: Fair; the separate package makes the named unsafe.Pointer conversion a direct compile-and-run integration check.
tests.verifies: Converting a named unsafe.Pointer value to *upInt yields the same address as the direct conversion and reads as upInt; converting to *int yields &n; writing through the view updates n; named array and struct views read named element/field types and convert back to the original addresses; and a zero upUnsafe converts to nil pointers of the tested types.
